name: Agriculture
blurb: Vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, and autonomous equipment at commercial scale, tracked through USDA ERS, FAO, satellite data providers, and the equipment and standards bodies.

points.desc: Deere's precision agriculture line (See and Spray, autonomous tractors) is the reference commercial deployment.
points.name: Precision ag is shipping product

points.desc: Census BTOS covers agriculture-adjacent sectors in its fortnightly AI-use series.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The Economic Research Service publishes the data series on precision-agriculture adoption across US farms - variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, autonomous equipment. The federal measurement layer.
points.name: USDA ERS measures US adoption

points.desc: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's digital agriculture program, with the 60 Decibels-supported Digital Agriculture Index, benchmarks platform adoption and real-world yield and income impact.
points.name: FAO benchmarks digital agriculture globally

points.desc: The AgriFoodTech investment research tracks venture capital into agricultural AI, robotics, computer vision, and farm-management software - the sector's funding barometer.
points.name: AgFunder indexes the investment flow

points.desc: Planet Labs' high-resolution imagery, Descartes Labs' geospatial ML, and EarthDaily's field-level crop indicators supply the AI-ready observation data behind yield prediction and crop-stress detection.
points.name: The satellite layer feeds the models

points.desc: The Association of Equipment Manufacturers covers autonomous machinery, AI hardware standards, and robotics adoption across crop and livestock production.
points.name: AEM tracks the machinery standards

points.desc: The nonprofit consortium sets the open data standards that let AI models ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites - the plumbing under everything else.
points.name: AgGateway makes the data interoperable

points.desc: The International Society of Precision Agriculture is the scientific organization connecting academic research on remote sensing and spatial analytics to commercial practice.
points.name: ISPA bridges the science and the field

points.desc: The 100 Million Farmers initiative tracks AI adoption through the lens of climate-smart and regenerative agriculture metrics globally.
points.name: WEF tracks climate-smart adoption

points.desc: Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular are the large digital-farming platforms turning soil, weather, and yield data into planting and input prescriptions with machine learning.
points.name: The agribusiness platforms run the prescriptions

points.desc: CNH Industrial's Raven division builds driverless tractor technology, AI path-planning, and precision application - the equipment layer beyond Deere.
points.name: CNH and Raven automate the other fleets

points.desc: Carbon Robotics' LaserWeeder kills weeds with computer vision and lasers instead of herbicide; Monarch builds electric driverless tractors - narrow AI shipping as farm equipment.
points.name: The pure-plays attack single problems

summary: Precision agriculture - vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, autonomous equipment - is deployed at commercial scale. Who tracks it: federal adoption data, a UN benchmarking framework, a venture index, and standards bodies, layered over the equipment giants and AI pure-plays actually shipping it.

analysis.body:
# Agriculture

Agriculture is measuring its adoption of AI through both public and private channels, though at modest levels by census standards. The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey suppressed its most recent reading for agriculture, but the prior period showed 13.7% of farms reporting AI use in the preceding two weeks. This snapshot captures a sector in transition from trial to deployment, with measurement infrastructure now in place through USDA ERS, which publishes data series on precision-agriculture adoption across US farms tracking variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, and autonomous equipment.

The capital flow into agrifoodtech reveals both selective momentum and geographic divergence. Per AgFunder, global agrifoodtech funding hit $16.2 billion in 2025, almost flat versus the prior year at a 3% decline, but investors are writing checks more selectively toward companies with tangible science and real unit economics. Development-market agrifoodtech grew substantially between 2023 and 2024, up 63% versus a 4% decline in global agrifoodtech overall. Asia-Pacific agrifoodtech raised $4.2 billion as of October 2024, a 38% increase on the $3.1 billion raised in the same period in 2023. African agrifoodtech raised $145 million in the first half of 2024, a 1.6% year-over-year increase, but remains a small fraction of global investment at 1.6%.

The deployed AI concentrates in two commercial layers: large platforms and narrow equipment. Per Climate FieldView's reporting, farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of 5 bu/ac compared to users who wrote their own scripts, providing direct ROI evidence on input optimization. Carbon Robotics positions its LaserWeeder and Carbon AI as autonomous farming solutions powered by a Large Plant Model trained on the world's largest agricultural dataset, deployed to reduce costs, eliminate weeds, increase yields, and improve farm sustainability. These deployments depend on data interoperability and satellite feeds. Per Planet Labs, its high-resolution daily Earth data, archive, and analytics give customers an unprecedented view to make decisions at the daily pace of change. AgGateway, a nonprofit, enables the industry's transition to digital agriculture through open data standards that let AI models ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites, with the Traceability Initiative in North America working on grain traceability and farm and crop field identification.

The scientific and standards infrastructure supporting AI deployment spans multiple organizations. The FAO's e-Agriculture program facilitates dialogue on the adoption and use of ICTs and digital innovations in agriculture globally, with the mission to facilitate discussion on adoption and use of ICTs and digital innovations in agriculture, forestry, fisheries, natural resource management and rural development. The International Society of Precision Agriculture, a scientific organization, develops solutions to feed the world with new technologies and has developed the Precision Agriculture Definition available in over fifteen languages. The Association of Equipment Manufacturers brings ag OEMs together to shape policy, understand data, and develop strategies to combat environmental, political, and economic changes facing agriculture, covering autonomous machinery and AI hardware standards.

Adoption pathways remain uneven across farm scale and geography, with measurement improving faster than deployment. The sources show capital flowing toward companies demonstrating unit economics rather than speculative ventures, seed-placement AI delivering quantified yield gains, and physical AI systems like autonomous weeders shipping as standalone farm equipment. What a prospective adopter should take from this is that the infrastructure for AI deployment—satellite data, open standards, equipment integration—is operational and vendor-backed, that on-farm economics are now measured rather than promised, and that adoption remains concentrated among larger operations and developed markets where data density and equipment compatibility enable integration.
